E1566.summary: In Eirenaeus, quoted by Atwood, what Argent Vive prepared by art gives: the mother of the Stone, known by several names.
E1566.body: Eirenaeus, quoted, says that Argent Vive prepared by art “gives the secret menstrual: The mother of our Stone which is so rare.” [III.1 ¶69] He gives it further names: “Our oil, our unguent, and our marchasite; Which we do name also our fountain bright.” [III.1 ¶69] So, in his verse, secret menstrual = mother of the Stone = oil, unguent, marchasite, fountain bright.

E1567.summary: The philosophers' name for what the Art teaches but never teaches openly; in Morieni, the magistery itself, God's secret.
E1567.body: Artephius, quoted, rebukes the literal reader: “you, fool, believe we teach the secret of secrets openly” [I.1 ¶84]. Atwood records Secretu Secretorum as a philosophers' name for the same thing, and cites Morieni identifying it with the magistery: “hoc magisterium nihil aliud est, nisi Arcanum et secretum secretorum Dei altissimi et magni” [II.4 ¶39] (our rendering: this magistery is nothing else but the Arcanum and secret of secrets of God most high and great). In Morieni, then, the secret of secrets = the magisterium, God's secret entrusted to the prophets [II.4 ¶39].

E1568.summary: What Form (Light) clothed with matter begets, impressing its character on matter; the seed of gold is called the Stone of Fire.
E1568.body: Atwood presents seed as what Form, or Light, begets when clothed with matter: “Which clothed with mater doth a seed beget.” [I.2 ¶45] The seed impresses its character on matter; metals arise from metalline seeds out of the Universal Spirit, while vulgar gold lacks seed until art helps it [I.2 ¶45]. An adept, cited by her, identifies the seed of gold with the Stone of Fire: “the seed of gold, says the adept, is a fiery form of Light inspissate, and this is the Stone of Fire” [I.2 ¶44].

E1569.summary: In Sendivogius, quoted, that of which man's body is a shadow.
E1569.body: Sendivogius, quoted, says “the body of man is a shadow of the seed of nature” [II.1 ¶10].

E1570.summary: What is at last found within the purified material extreme of this life, described as a heavy, decompounded ens shining like a fiery star.
E1570.body: Atwood: “within the material extreme of this life, when it is purified, the Seed of Spirit is at last found” [II.3 ¶30]. It is described there as a heavy, decompounded ens shining like a fiery star [II.3 ¶30].

E1571.summary: The active principle whose Will the Passive Intelligence answers and accompanies through the abyss.
E1571.body: Atwood speaks of the Passive Intelligence which “responds to the Will of her seeking Reason” [III.1 ¶40]; the seeking Reason is the active partner (spoken of as him), which she accompanies through the abyss.

E1573.summary: This life of ours, in which the Divine Light is hidden and which appropriates that Light instead of serving it.
E1573.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls our life self-begotten, the life in which the Divine Light is hidden: “This life of ours, instead of administering to the Divine Life, appropriates it.” [APP ¶70]

E1574.summary: Centers that gifted beings in whom the Word gives power tend to set up; key to the Second Commandment as the result of violating the First.
E1574.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood warns that “the danger is the tendency in such gifted beings to set up self-centers” [APP ¶100], beings in whom the Word gives power. She treats this as the key to the Second Commandment, as the outcome of violating the First [APP ¶100].

E1575.summary: What adulterates vision in the phantastic sphere.
E1575.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says of vision in the phantastic sphere: “it is self-desire that adulterates” [APP ¶105].

E1576.summary: Atwood's name for the Hermetic method itself: inner revelation in a purified soul, the root of alchemical tradition and the narrow way of regeneration.
E1576.body:
For Atwood, Self-Knowledge is the Hermetic method: “the Hermetic method of Self-Knowledge” [I.3 n46], which alone enables man to know, understand and possess divine things. She holds “Self-Knowledge to be at the root of all Alchemical tradition” [II.1 ¶30], formerly taken as a way to knowledge of Universal Nature.

It is the object of the inward search whose method she seeks from the ancients: “the true method and conditions of Self- Knowledge” [II.1 ¶46]. She sets it apart from trance or vision and equates it with the true psychical experience: “For it is this, no common trance or day-dream, or any fanatical vision of celestials, that we propose to scrutinize, but the true psychical experience” [II.1 ¶46].

It is among the goods of the higher Mysteries: “the Self-Knowledge and perfection of life and immortality promised” [II.2 ¶7]. Atwood names by it the method of inner revelation in a purified soul, “the narrow way of regeneration into life” [II.4 ¶19]. The Greeks reached “an experimental conception of its reality in the self-knowledge” [III.2 ¶46], i.e. of the reality of the Whole. Its condition is total privation: “Self-knowledge is impossible unless every other knowledge is deprived” [III.2 ¶56].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “Self-knowledge is the first contact of consciousness in the ground of life.” [APP ¶137]

E1577.summary: That through which the Reason arises, with creative attributes and powers, in regeneration.
E1577.body: Atwood says the Reason “arises through the self-perceivance, with creative attributes and powers” [III.3 ¶52]. Whose self is perceived the text does not specify here.

E1578.summary: The individual's distinct subsistence as separated, or outborn, from the Fontal Reason.
E1578.body: Atwood describes the individual as “a distinct self-spiration, severation, or outbirth, as it were, from that Fontal Reason” [III.3 ¶52]: self-spiration is thus equated with severation and outbirth.

E1579.summary: The forbidden regions into which depraved minds climbed by the clue of life.
E1579.body: Atwood says depraved minds, given the clue of life, “climbed by it into forbidden regions of self-sufficiency” [III.4 ¶4].

E1580.summary: The individual, self-centred will acting for itself rather than under God's law, at war with the Divine Will; to be brought into subjection.
E1580.body:
All records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood describes self-will as will acting for itself rather than under God's law: “The magic of the self-will is that which the Egyptians practiced in the days of Moses” [APP ¶2], and power “taken into the self-will and used accordingly it becomes diabolical” [APP ¶4].

When the Wisdom-life is stirred, “what takes it is the self-will” [APP ¶82]; it wars with the Universal Will and, as patient, has its false forms dissolved. Drawn upward by love it becomes passive; acting before its time it destroys: “There is a swiftness in the self-willed magnet working powerfully and to destruction” [APP ¶103]. The Divine purpose is to “bring the self-willed opposition into subjection” [APP ¶104], through man's consent. In religion it distorts: “The action of the self-will on the soul which exaggerates its religious life” [APP ¶110].

It is the principle we are born into: “This war is the war between two principles of the self-will and the Divine Will.” [APP ¶154]

E1581.summary: The inner self-will that arrests the entering light; it must be humbled by voluntary sacrifice and is finally subdued by the connate spirit.
E1581.body: Atwood describes the light “penetrating to meet the self-willed Identity within, is arrested” [III.1 ¶53]. This Identity must be humbled by voluntary sacrifice, “humiliation of the Selfhood under the exemplary cross of Christ” [III.1 ¶60], and the connate spirit at last subdues it to self-mortification [III.1 ¶60].

E1582.summary: The separate, self-centred individual self into which the soul has fallen; it must be dissolved, subverted and abandoned to the Divine Will for regeneration.
E1582.body:
Atwood treats selfhood as the separate self that must be undone. Its “dark dominion” [II.3 n2] is dissolved by the magnetic friction of its proper light. Reiterated reflexive analysis serves so that “it may resolve the separable Selfhood” [IV.1 ¶20]; rectification and sublimation are completed “by an actual subversion of the selfhood” [IV.1 ¶47]. The work requires one “to abandon the life of selfhood” [III.4 ¶6], the necessary charges, and return to the Universal by “abandoning the selfhood” [IV.4 ¶27]. Immortality is consummated by “the abandonment of the dual selfhood and its volition to the Divine Will” [IV.3 ¶58]; then “from the separable selfhood, the Identity passes into universal accord” [IV.3 ¶60].

In III.2 (voice unclear) the selfhood is obliterated in the attraction into the First Cause: “as this selfhood likewise is obliterated in the overwhelming attraction, which raises it into the First Cuase” [III.2 ¶56]; and non-being is glossed as the subjective selfhood, whose additions bring poverty [III.2 ¶59].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) the soul's fall is “the fall away of it into selfhood, which has defaced the image” [APP ¶120], and the converting light shines on “the darkness of the selfhood on which it shines” [APP ¶114]. The Midas-will holds the life it possesses “holding it as he did the selfhood” [APP ¶159].

forms: the author of the New Light
E1583.summary: An adept and author of the New Light of Alchemy, among Atwood's most cited and generally endorsed authorities on the matter, water and practice of the Art.
E1583.body:
Atwood names him Michael Sendivogius, author of Novum Lumen Chemicum / The New Light of Alchemy; his imprisonment illustrates persecution, and his book is praised as attractive but deliberately disordered, needing repeated study; some identify him with Philalethes and with Alexander Seton [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶71, I.1 ¶73].

On method of reading: from his Preface, one must read from the possibility of nature, not the words, for “this Art is for the wise, not for the ignorant” [I.1 ¶84]; from his Epilogue, philosophers teach indirectly and contradict on purpose, “it being the custom of philosophers to use them; thou hast need of them” [I.1 ¶84].

On the matter: “Our water is heavenly, not wetting the hands, not of the vulgar, but almost rain water” [I.2 ¶33]; his saying that the matter of metals is twofold Atwood reinterprets as relation within the Ethereal being [I.2 ¶42]. One must seek the hidden thing yielding a moisture “which doth dissolve gold without violence or noise” [I.2 ¶48]. “Vulgar gold Sendivogius compares to a herb without seed” [I.2 ¶49]. The three principles are one substance in triple relation, “a body, a spirit, and an occult soul” [I.3 n30]; and “our lune or silver, not common silver, is that which receives the seed of the gold” [I.3 n39]. He describes the Water of our Sea, “that water was as white as snow” [III.2 ¶7], “the water of our sea, the water of life, not wetting the hands” [III.2 n43]; and the enigmatic conversion of elements: “who knows how to congeal water with heat, and to join a spirit thereto” [III.3 ¶29].

Atwood criticizes him once as diverting readers from Morien's hint [II.1 ¶8], but endorses him on man as microcosm: “the soul in man, the lesser world or microcosm, substituting the place of its center, is the king” [II.1 ¶10]; on Fire: “Fire, says the adept philosopher, is the purest and most worthy of all the elements” [II.4 ¶39]; and on prayer with work: “Pray, says Sendivogius, pray; but work.” [III.4 ¶20]. He also supplies “Urinus Saturni” for the Black Saturn [II.3 ¶18], his Planetary Sphere = the seven mystic mountains [II.4 ¶9], and the fight in which “Sal gave Sulfur a mortal wound” [III.1 ¶56], yielding white milk [III.1 n62]; per n66 he is also the source of the Adept's saying that without Salt no man attains the Science [III.1 n66]. His friends disbelieved that “there was any water in our sea” [III.4 ¶16]. In IV.3, the wary Artist, he teaches spiritual fermentation: “thou takest not common gold or silver, for these are dead; take Ours which are living” [IV.3 ¶21], admitting that his experience stopped there. In the Appendix (later layer) he is cited for the Philosopher who “looks not out on nature with the eyes of common men” [APP ¶67].

E1584.summary: Cited, from his Epistola xci, as witness to Democritus' making of artificial precious stones.
E1584.body: Atwood cites Seneca (Epistola xci) for Democritus' “his artificial confection of precious stones” [I.1 ¶12, I.1 n18].

E1585.summary: Cited for the precept that the volatile must be united with the fixed, which Atwood says deserves attention.
E1585.body: Atwood cites Senior's precept on uniting volatile with fixed, “the highest fume should be reduced to the lowest” [IV.3 ¶8], as one which deserves attention.

E1586.summary: Sense perception and its beguilements, made the beacon of modern thought; the turbulent sea beyond which the haven lies.
E1586.body: Atwood laments that modern thought follows “the beguilements of sense” [IV.4 ¶28] and places the haven “beyond the turbulent sea of sense” [IV.4 ¶32].

E1587.summary: The medium of sense-consciousness that trance dissolves, beneath which consciousness is later translated.
E1587.body: Atwood says trance can “dissolve the sensible medium and convert it to the experience of another life” [II.3 ¶5]; consciousness is afterwards translated beneath it.

E1588.summary: What is fixed and must be dissolved in the work.
E1588.body: Atwood glosses the alchemical fixed thing as the sensual compact: “that which was fixed, viz., the sensual compact, is dissolved” [II.3 ¶37].

E1589.summary: The dominance of sense-life, identified with the corporeal; softened by the ethereal waters and subdued by Spirit in regeneration.
E1589.body: Atwood says the ethereal waters soften the sensual dominant to “make it more fit for the returning reason and understanding to work upon” [III.1 ¶53]. It is subdued “when the sensual dominant is occultated in the Divine Fiat and subdued” [III.3 ¶15], and she identifies it with the corporeal: Spirit “overcomes the corporeal, which is the sensual dominant, in the regeneration” [III.3 ¶23].

E1590.summary: What is without a person; it must be made flexible and hidden.
E1590.body: Atwood glosses that which is without: “that which is without, viz., the sensual spirit of life must be made flexible and occultated” [I.3 n8].

E1591.summary: The principle of sense in the blood, dissolved by magnetizing and reiterated contritions; its residuum supplies body to the regenerate soul.
E1591.body: Both records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood identifies it as “the principle of sense or the sensuous medium in the blood” [APP ¶109], against which the senses are turned. Absorbed by reiterative contritions and dissolved by magnetizing, “it dissolved the sensuous medium and opens the consciousness to the Divine life” [APP ¶91]. Brought to its last ens, “The residuum from this medium supplies body to the regenerate soul” [APP ¶110].

E1592.summary: The spirit in the blood through which life acts; taken up into the will, it dies so that new life, the Phoenix, may arise.
E1592.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood describes the spirit in the blood through which life acts, to be taken up into the will so that new life grows from its death: “Out of the ashes of this present sensuous spirit arises the Phoenix.” [APP ¶91]

E1593.summary: In Atwood's modern exponent, what was at first fixed and is dissolved in the blackening.
E1593.body: Quoting our modern exponent, Atwood reports that in the blackening “that which at first was fixed, viz., the sentient medium, is dissolved” [II.1 ¶23].

E1594.summary: The primary object of the Art: separating pure from impure and subtle from gross, which Atwood takes to be apparently identical with the Mysteries' ordeal of the death of the natural life.
E1594.body:
Paracelsus, quoted, held that “separation was the principle and beginning of all generation” [I.2 ¶25], the greatest miracle in philosophy; it is the first half of Ripley's procedure before recombination [I.2 ¶25].

Atwood: “This Separation is indeed the primary object of the Art” [III.1 ¶21], the separating of pure from impure and subtle from gross, done by mind, not mechanical dissolution. She identifies it with the Mysteries: it “appears to be identical with that which is described as taking place in the Mysteries, when the great ordeals are passed through during the decomposition and death of the natural life” [III.1 ¶21].

E1595.summary: The true separating agent, whose finding is the greatest difficulty; in Boehme, a divine artist of great subtlety within lovers of the Art.
E1595.body: Atwood: “To find the true Separator is described, in fact, as the greatest difficulty” [III.1 ¶32], which she likens to Virgil's hidden tree. Jacob Boehme, quoted, speaks of lovers of the Art “whose Separator is an artist of great subtlety in them” [III.1 ¶39], a divine agent that must not be given into the bestial hand.

E1596.summary: In the Adept's words, the seven made when Three and Four unite; the true Sabaoth, the rest of God the creature shall enter.
E1596.body: The Adept, quoted: “Three and Four make seven.” [IV.2 ¶18] (the four elements with Unity and Ternarius). He identifies it: “This Sepentary is the true Sabaoth, the rest of God” [IV.2 ¶18], which the creature shall enter.
